description: A pie chart is a circular statistical graph divided into sectors to illustrate numerical proportion. The entire circle represents 100% or 360 degrees of the total quantity.

sections.title: Basic Concepts
sections.description: Understanding the main components of a pie chart and their characteristics is essential for solving questions.

key_concepts.explanation: The entire circle represents the total sum of the given data.
Each part of the circle represents a specific category. Its size is proportional to the value of that category.
This is the angle subtended by a sector at the center of the circle. The sum of all central angles is 360°.

sections.title: Important Formulas
sections.description: Essential mathematical formulas for conversion between angles, percentages, and actual values.

equations: Central Angle = (Value of Category / Total Value) * 360°
Value of Category = (Central Angle / 360) * Total Value

sections.title: Steps to Solve Questions
sections.description: A systematic method to solve pie chart questions with accuracy and speed in exams.

steps.title: Identify the Base
steps.detail: Check whether the pie chart is given in Percentage (total 100%) or Degree (total 360°). Also, note down the Total Value.

steps.title: Analyze Asked Data
steps.detail: Find the value or ratio of the specific sector or category asked in the question.

steps.title: Use Direct Calculation
steps.detail: If the difference or sum between two categories is asked, first subtract/add their percentages or degrees, then multiply by the total value at once. (Avoid calculating separately)

sections.title: Types Asked in Exams
sections.description: Different formats of pie charts that appear in competitive exams.

results: Calculations are straightforward and based on a single total value.
Two circles are given for comparison between two different years or categories.
Students must pay attention to the different base values of both charts.
The pie chart gives the total distribution, and the table gives its sub-division (e.g., male/female ratio).
This is the most complex type where both graphs must be read together.
